children: The founder of private-stock investment firm Linqto has been charged with defrauding tens of thousands of investors to whom he marketed investments in shares of pre-IPO companies.

Linqto founder William Sarris is accused of manufacturing false scarcity of private company shares to drive up prices. Prosecutors allege he pushed markups beyond what his own lawyers warned him was lawful to boost his company's revenue.
He was charged this week with securities fraud, broker-dealer fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy. A lawyer for Sarris said he "is innocent of these charges and intends to fight them."
Another former Linqto executive, Joseph Endoso, pleaded guilty in connection with his participation in the scheme at Linqto and is cooperating with the government, the prosecutors said.

The Wall Street Journal wrote about Sarris' alleged "guerrilla" tactics in selling pre-IPO shares last summer, noting that the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department were looking into Linqto and its founder.

The conversation around the risks involved in private-market investing has only gotten louder since then. SEC examiners have been asking registered investment advisers for proof that their investment funds own or have exposure to the shares in private companies that they claim to, the Journal reported earlier this week.
One such fund touted pre-IPO exposure to SpaceX but later told investors the shares were sold before the company went public, limiting investors' expected gains, the Journal recently reported.

Linqto has been under new management since January 2025 and began cooperating with the SEC investigation at that point, the Journal has reported. The Justice Department launched its own criminal probe in early 2025.
The firm filed for bankruptcy protection last year to protect customer assets, citing investigations into its business and questions about what its customers owned.
